name: podcast
hook: I ran this podcast through a live claim meter.

questions.label: Factual claim
questions.instructions: Does `sentence` state a specific fact about the past or present that could be checked?

true.means: A checkable number, date, study, event or named fact.
examples: The first iPhone launched in 2007.
Norway gets over 90 percent of its power from hydro.

false.means: An opinion, feeling, preference, story or claim too vague to check.
examples: That was our best episode.
People underestimate farming.

questions.label: Unsupported claim
questions.instructions: Does `sentence` assert a factual-sounding claim as true without any evidence, source or reasoning?

true.means: A confident factual claim with nothing behind it.
examples: Seed oils are why everyone is sick.
Cold showers double testosterone, that's a fact.

false.means: A personal preference, clearly hedged opinion, cited evidence, or a plain story.
examples: I prefer running in the morning.
A 2019 meta-analysis found a small effect.
I've read claims it helps, not sure.

questions.label: Overgeneralization
questions.instructions: Does `sentence` itself endorse a sweeping, unqualified claim about a broad group of people or things (a stereotype-like all / every / nobody / always / never)?

true.means: The speaker asserts, as their own view, that a whole broad group always or never is or does something.
examples: Every founder is a narcissist.
Nobody under thirty reads anymore.
Doctors never listen.

false.means: Any of: a hedged quantifier (most, many, a lot of, some); the speaker's own habits; a literal statement about a small, defined set (this season's episodes, our team); reporting or rebutting someone else's generalization; a specific person.
examples: Most people I talk to are burned out.
I always record the intro last.
Every episode this season was recorded in Denver.
Critics say nobody watches TV, but the ratings disagree.

questions.label: Emotional appeal
questions.instructions: Does `sentence` rely mainly on outrage, fear or ridicule rather than evidence?

true.means: Its force comes from making the listener angry, afraid or contemptuous.
examples: If this doesn't make you furious you're not paying attention.
Imagine being so stupid you believe that.

false.means: It is informational, analytical, or shares a personal feeling without inflaming the listener.
examples: The ruling hinges on the 1996 statute.
Her story moved me.

questions.label: Self-promotion
questions.instructions: Is `sentence` promoting the speaker's own or a sponsor's product, course, newsletter or brand?

true.means: An ad read, sponsor mention, discount code, or plug for the speaker's own offering.
examples: My course goes live Monday, link below.
Use code CAST for 20 percent off.

false.means: It recommends someone else's free resource, thanks the host, or talks about the speaker's past.
examples: There's a great free MIT textbook.
Thanks for having me.
